Project overview

Bringing a complex enterprise procurement platform to mobile.

My role
UX Designer & Researcher
Platform
Mobile — iOS & Android
Outcome
Role-based mobile app with task-first navigation, live in production

IENT is an enterprise procurement platform: the system a large company uses to buy what it needs and manage its vendors. Separate apps cover each step of buying, from requisitions, RFQs and auctions to purchase orders, receipts and invoices, plus vendor registration and ratings. Every document carries a status, a history and a next action, and all of it runs on the web.

Business requirement

Mobile is needed

IENT ran only on the web.

IENT serves two kinds of user: those who raise records and those who approve them. In procurement, every step depends on the one before it. An order can’t be released until its request is approved, and a vendor can’t be paid until the invoice is reviewed. So when either user is away from a desk, everything queued behind their decision stops.

IENT moved at the speed of its decisions, but those decisions were tied to a desktop. Approvals, invoice reviews, and order releases all had to wait until decision-makers were back at their desks.
Objective

Enable users to take critical actions anywhere, stay informed, and keep procurement moving without being tied to a desktop.

Approach

Considered

Make the web platform responsive

The obvious solution was to make the web platform responsive: shrink columns, stack sidebars, and hide what didn’t fit. It was the fastest way to bring the existing interface to mobile.

Why we rejected it

Responsive fits the web onto a phone, but it doesn’t serve the objective. Decisions stay several screens deep, staying informed still means opening a browser, and effort spreads to surfaces that never slow procurement down.

Actions are still buried

Responsive design preserves access to every web action, but not the speed of acting. Approvals remain buried several screens deep, and records show more information than needed to make a decision. It fits the phone, but it isn’t built for speed.

Updates wait to be found

Staying informed requires the product to reach the user. A responsive site waits to be opened, often behind a sign-in screen, leaving users dependent on what they remember to check.

Decisions get no priority

Procurement stalls on decisions, not on reports or settings. Responsive treats every screen the same, so decisions get no special attention.

What we did instead

Instead of shrinking the whole platform, we gave mobile a narrower job: put decisions within reach, bring updates to the user, and leave the depth work on the web.

This way, we also stay true to the objective.

Design principle

This approach gave mobile a distinct position in relation to the web:

the mobile app would be a companion to the web, not a replacement for it.

With mobile defined as a companion, the question changed from what can fit on a phone to what deserves to be there. That gave every later decision a clear boundary.

The decision framework

To apply the principle consistently, we turned it into three questions. Instead of judging features one by one, we mapped the entire product against them to see what genuinely belonged on mobile.

01

Would having this on mobile save real time?

When a task depends on someone acting from a desktop, the whole process waits for them.

Moving these to mobile removes the wait. Tasks that don't have anyone waiting on them don't need to move.

For example
  • An approval waiting for the approver
  • A request waiting to be raised
02

Does it move procurement forward?

Some tasks push a record to its next step, like acting on what's urgent. Others are for reference, like checking a record's history or tracing what changed. Reference work matters, but nothing moves forward because of it.

For example
  • Acting on what's urgent
  • Staying aware of what's pending
03

How often does it come up?

Frequent tasks justify the cost of a second interface, both to build and to learn. Rare ones don't — the user will be at a desk when they do them anyway.

For example
  • Checking your to-dos
  • Replying to a vendor

User persona

Understanding the users before designing for them.

Three roles use IENT — Initiator, Approver, and Administrator. Each does a different job on the platform, and mobile had to serve each one differently.

01
On mobile
Role 01

Initiator

Creates and manages procurement records

Can do
  • Create records (PO, PR, RFQ, Auction)
  • Manage and edit existing records
  • Communicate with vendors
  • Submit records for approval
02
On mobile
Role 02

Approver

Reviews and approves submitted records

Can do
  • Approve, Reject, or Return records
  • Comment and request amendments
  • Delegate to another approver when unavailable
  • View full record history
  • Nudge initiators for updates
03
Web only
Role 03

Administrator

Manages users, access, and system config

Can do
  • Manage user roles and permissions
  • Configure approval workflows
  • View all records across roles
  • Generate system-wide reports
A note on the Administrator role

The Administrator role was deliberately excluded from V1 — and the decision came directly from the design principle. Administrator tasks are system configuration, user permissions, and settings management. Important work, but not time-sensitive, and not what stalls the procurement process. Held against the two tests — does this help the user act right now, does this help the procurement process move forward faster — the Administrator role didn't clear either bar. It stayed on the web, where it belongs.

Research

What competitor apps revealed.

Before committing to a direction, competitor apps were studied to understand how mobile procurement and enterprise workflows are handled in shipped products.

Research methodology

Competitor apps were studied through official demo videos, help documentation and product walkthroughs. Organisational licensing ruled out direct access, but the videos showed enough of each app's structure and interactions.

Competitive analysis, app by app

SAP Ariba
+Pros

Clear primary information. Buttons placed correctly and easy to reach. Good status visibility.

!Learning

Unclear icons. Text layout breaks on long content.

What IENT took

Pinned Take Action full-width to the bottom. Text labels alongside status chips. Collapsible sections to handle long content gracefully.

EquipMe
+Pros

Clear primary information. Good status visibility on record cards.

!Learning

Buttons not prominent. Spacing not distributed properly. Edit and delete not accessible enough.

What IENT took

Status chips on list cards. Take Action in a dedicated pinned position, not inline with content.

Oracle
+Pros

Clear action confirmation message. Good status visibility.

!Learning

Buttons not prominent. Inconsistent typography. Limited actionability.

What IENT took

Single prominent always-visible action button. Clear post-approval state with visible status change.

Coupa
+Pros

Clear grouped layout. Toggle for binary fields is space-efficient.

!Learning

Visual hierarchy not differentiated. Fields appear visually similar. Action buttons too subtle.

What IENT took

Collapsible sections grouped by category. Distinct visual weight for status, separate from other fields.

Patterns catalogued across all apps

01

Tab-based navigation

At app level for module switching, and within records for Details, Attachments, and Conversations.

02

Primary actions separated from content

Placed outside the scrollable area, so always visible and reachable.

03

Progressive disclosure on complex records

Collapsible sections rather than one continuous scroll.

04

Mobile experience centred around action

Approving, rejecting, filling, and submitting forms, not detailed review or administrative tasks.

Information Architecture

Structural decisions before the screens.

The tab navigation structure and the record detail hierarchy were established before any hi-fi screens were drawn. The IA defined what could live on mobile and what had to stay on web.

Web4 top-level destinations4 tiers deepa full procurement workspaceWeb only

Built for heavy work. The web structure carries the heavy work, so it goes deep and stays ordered. Depth here reads as organization, not distance.

Administration stripped, action paths shortened
Mobile4 top-level destinationsrecord actions preservednothing administrative

Built for action. The mobile structure exists to act on work, not administer it. So it keeps only the path to what's waiting, and leaves everything else on the web.

Final Design

Four modules, one mobile app

The web has room to hold everything. A phone doesn't, and shouldn't. So mobile was built around two aims: get to the task and act, fast — and work as a companion to the web, not a replacement for it. Configuration and reporting stay on the desktop. Mobile carries only what's needed to monitor, decide, and move on.

Initiator · Home

A shorter path to the day's work

The aim of the Home screen was to reduce unnecessary repetitive navigation and provide a seamless desktop-to-mobile switch. Both aims apply equally to both roles.

  • Reduce repetitive navigation — achieved through the Quick Actions and In Progress sections, which bring the user's most frequent tasks and ongoing work to the surface, one tap away.
  • Seamless desktop-to-mobile switch — achieved through the Last Visited section, which lets a user pick up on the phone exactly where they left off on the desktop.
1

Quick Access

Creating new requests is the initiator's most frequent task, yet reaching the right module often takes several navigation steps.

Home→Apps→Select Module→Create record

By placing role-specific shortcuts where users first land, repetitive tasks start in a single tap, cutting out the trip through the Apps section.

Home→Create record

A shorter path for everyday tasks, while Apps stays the place to explore every module. It makes Home a surface built for speed.

2

Last Visited

Users revisit the same records throughout a procurement workflow. Surfacing the last opened record on Home removes the walk back through the modules, so they regain context at once.

Before
Home→Apps→Select Module→Locate Record
After
Home→Last Visited Record
3

In Progress

Procurement tasks are rarely finished in one sitting. Users pause while waiting on information or approvals, so drafts are a natural part of the work. Gathering every draft under In Progress lets them pick up where they left off.

Before
Home→Apps→Select Module→Draft Records
After
Home→In Progress
Approver · Home

Overview in place of Quick Actions

The same two aims apply for Approvers, with one addition — Approvers also monitor procurement health. So alongside surfacing pending records to review, the Home screen brings up an overview of critical activities such as pending payments and expiring contracts, so users can quickly see what needs attention and act on it.

1

Overview, not Quick Actions

An approver's job is to monitor, not to create records or raise requests. So the top of Home carries a glimpse of activity that could compromise procurement health if left unnoticed: payments still pending, contracts near expiry, and other signals worth acting on.

2

Last Visited

Users revisit the same records throughout a procurement workflow. Surfacing the last opened record on Home removes the walk back through the modules, so they regain context at once.

3

Recents

The five most recently arrived tasks awaiting the approver's action. Unlike To-do's, which is opened when the approver decides to work through the queue, Recents keeps them aware of what has landed the moment they open the app — a passive glance rather than an active review.

Initiator · To-do's

The whole queue, built to be narrowed

The goal for To-do's was to reorganize the existing experience for mobile, not redesign the workflow. Two things followed:

  • Reprioritize what each row shows so the most useful details surface first.
  • Recognize that users aren't browsing but finding one task. Search, filter, and sort were placed within immediate reach, so narrowing the queue takes minimal effort.
1

Search and filters within immediate reach

A user opening To-do's isn't scanning the queue; they're finding one task. So search and filters are pinned near the top, ahead of the list itself. The list is a fallback, not the starting point.

2

Rows are cards now, grouped by day

Each item is a card carrying the fields that matter most at a glance: type and ID, title, current status, and how long it has waited. It's enough to judge whether the record needs opening. The cards are grouped by day, so the freshest work sits at the top without asking the user to sort. A tap takes them straight into the record.

  • Recognize that users aren't browsing but finding one task. Search, filter, and sort were placed within immediate reach, so narrowing the queue takes minimal effort.

Initiator · Apps

Every module, one entry point

Apps is a place which shows the full catalogue of Apps/Modules. It also shows quick action and active records for initiator.

1

Grouped by stage

On the web, modules are listed alphabetically. On mobile, they're grouped by procurement stage: sourcing apps first, then purchasing, then what comes after.

2

Approver · Apps

Every module, one entry point

Apps is a place which shows the full catalogue of Apps/Modules. It also shows records that are awaiting action for approver.

1

Grouped by stage

On the web, modules are listed alphabetically. On mobile, they're grouped by procurement stage: sourcing apps first, then purchasing, then what comes after.

2

Awaiting Action Records

For the approver, each row shows the number of records currently awaiting their action. It's a quick signal of where decisions are pending, so an empty count means nothing needs reviewing.

Initiator · Updates

What changed while you were away

On the web, updates live behind the bell icon. They can be read, but not acted on. On mobile, updates get their own section, and every update opens the record it refers to.

Updates carries only what keeps the user informed: status changes and conversation activity. Tasks are deliberately left out, since mixing them in would clutter the feed. They live in To-do's instead, where they can be worked through as a queue.

The separation makes both surfaces sharper. Opening Updates gives a quick read on what has changed, without the weight of a task list. Opening To-do's shows the work waiting, without status noise on top of it.

1

Two kinds, one feed

  • Conversation updates — replies from any user on any record.
  • Status updates — state changes of any record.
Approver · Updates

The same feed, scoped to the role

On the web, updates live behind the bell icon. They can be read, but not acted on. On mobile, updates get their own section, and every update opens the record it refers to.

Updates carries only what keeps the user informed: status changes and conversation activity. Tasks are deliberately left out, since mixing them in would clutter the feed. They live in To-do's instead, where they can be worked through as a queue.

The separation makes both surfaces sharper. Opening Updates gives a quick read on what has changed, without the weight of a task list. Opening To-do's shows the work waiting, without status noise on top of it.

Same structure, the approver's events

The feed keeps its shape. The approver sees the notifications and conversations tied to their decisions, in place of the initiator's.

Getting to a record

Three screens from opening the app to acting on a record

Most work on mobile ends at a single record. Reaching one runs through three screens: choose the app, find the record in its list, then open it.

1 2 3 4 5
1
1 2 3 4
1 2
Initiator · Record list

Narrowing to one

On the web, opening an app takes the user to a list of records for that app. From the list, they choose a record to view its detail. The same flow carries to mobile, but the surface is rebuilt for the phone.

1

The tabs give way to a back button

One level into an app, the bottom tabs are removed so nothing competes with the record for the screen. Moving sideways to another module is no longer the point; the way out is backwards, whether through the back button at the top or a swipe from the edge.

2

Filters at the top, not the edge

On the web, filter and search sit at the edge of the table. On mobile they move to the top of the list as chips, in front of the records rather than beside them.

3

Cards, not table rows

The list is rebuilt as a stack of cards. Each card carries the record ID, the title, the status, and when it was created. Where a record is tied to a vendor, the vendor name appears too. The structure lets the user scan and decide before opening.

4

One tap to the record

Tapping a card opens the record detail directly. The list is the entry point, not the destination.

5

Pagination pinned, not buried

On the web, the page controls sit at the very bottom of the table, found only after scrolling past the full list. On mobile they are pinned in place, so moving between pages does not depend on reaching the end first.

Approver · Record list

The same list, different records

The record list works the same way for the approver. What changes is which records fill it.

1

Same structure, different queue

The approver sees the same list layout as the initiator. What changes is the content: records awaiting review or approval rather than records the user created.

Initiator · Record detail

Where the decision happens

On the web, the record opens in read mode, and any change begins with the edit button. Mobile keeps that model. The record is where the initiator reviews what they submitted and, when needed, edits it.

1

ID, title, status, in that order of prominence

  • The record ID sits at the very top as the most prominent element, where on the web the ID is highlighted too.
  • The title sits directly below the ID in its own prominent place, where on the web it sits inside the details tab.
  • The status follows as a full width banner, where on the web it reads as ordinary text.
  • Ranking the three by prominence lets the user know what the record is and where it stands before reading a single field.
2

Only the tabs mobile needs

  • Four tabs carry the record: details, line items, attachments, and conversations, where the web spreads it across more, including workflow.
  • The user toggles between them.
  • The heavier tabs stay on the web, in keeping with the principle that mobile is for action, not administration.
3

Edit stays behind a button

  • The record opens read only and editing begins with the edit button, the same as the web.
  • On the web the edit button sits in the top corner, where on mobile it stays pinned within reach at the bottom.
  • Keeping the model the initiator already knows means nothing changes by accident and edit mode is entered deliberately.
4

The action stays in reach

  • Take Action stays pinned at the bottom across every scroll.
  • The action adapts to the tab where it is needed, and stays pinned wherever it appears.
Approver · Record detail

Reviewing and acting

1

The same record, a different task

The approver sees the same record detail layout. The difference is in the action: where an initiator edits or resubmits, the approver reviews and decides.

2

Take Action adapts to role

The pinned action bar at the bottom offers role-appropriate options — approve, reject, or return — rather than the initiator's edit and submit controls.

Mobile pattern

One surface, three jobs: the bottom sheet

Filtering, choosing an action, and inspecting a line item are all things a user does to a record. On web each was solved separately; on mobile they resolve to one pattern.

Web

Each job had its own component

Filters opened a panel, a line item expanded in a side panel, an action came up in a pop-up or dropdown. On a large screen that variety works.

The mobile problem

That variety breaks down

Replicating it would mean four different ways to bring up content on one small screen — inconsistent to learn and cramped to fit. What helped on web becomes friction on mobile.

Common thread

All three act on the record

Each is done to a record, and none is a reason to leave it — you filter the list you're on, act on the record you're reading, inspect a line item within it.

The pattern

One bottom sheet

It slides up over the record, holds whatever the job needs — filters, a decision, or a full line-item detail — and dismisses back to where you were. One consistent interaction, three different needs.

Bottom sheet · Filter

Narrowing without leaving the list

Tapping a filter chip above the list opens a sheet rather than a new screen. The filter options sit inside it — scrollable, with Clear and Apply.

The list stays in view

The sheet overlays the list instead of replacing it, so records narrow in view as filters are set — the user adjusts and sees the effect in one place, rather than committing blind and navigating back to check.

Grouped, and room to grow

Status, Saved View and Date sit in one scrollable sheet that expands as the option set grows, so the pattern doesn't break as filters multiply.

Commit or clear in place

Sticky Clear and Apply keep the primary actions reachable without scrolling or leaving the sheet.

Bottom sheet · Action

A container that flexes to the decision

Tapping the action bar on a record opens a sheet with the actions available for it. A record can carry many possible statuses, and the set shown depends on where the record stands.

The record stays behind

The sheet opens over the record, so the user acts on it without leaving what they're acting on — the context stays in view above the sheet.

The set isn't fixed

Different records and states surface different actions. The sheet presents whatever applies, as distinct tappable choices, without the user hunting through menus.

Some actions need more than a tap

A return requires a justification before it can be set. When that happens, the sheet opens an input field in the same place — a short decision and a longer form share one container, without covering the record or switching screens.

Bottom sheet · Line item details

Inspecting many, one after another

Tapping a line item opens its full detail in a sheet instead of navigating to a separate screen.

Opened in place

Tapping a line item opens its detail in a sheet, not a separate screen — the record header stays visible, so the user never loses their place.

Dismiss back to the list

Closing the sheet returns the user straight to the list, so checking five items is five taps — not five round-trips out to a detail screen and back.

Full detail, one surface

Material, tax and delivery all sit in the one sheet, scrollable, so the whole line item reads without leaving the record.

Outcomes & Reflection

What this project delivered.

The structures and patterns this design work produced, and the reasoning that holds them together.

→

Actions resolve in one sheet

Approve, return, or reject happen in a single bottom sheet over the record — and a return opens its reason field in the same place. No separate confirmation screen, no lost context.

✓

Core sections one or two taps away

A four-tab bottom bar — Home, To-do's, Apps, Updates — keeps every primary destination shallow.

◆

Role-scoped home screens

Separate Initiator and Approver home screens — action-first for both, structured around their different jobs.

↔

One record pattern across apps

The same record structure and action pattern carries across the platform's record apps — PR, PO, RFQ, Auction, and beyond — so learning one means knowing the rest.

≡

Filtering built for narrowing

Quick-access chips, grouped Status, Saved View and Date filters, and a sticky Clear / Apply — tuned for narrowing a queue, not building a query.

◐

Updates as its own surface

Distinct card types replace a flat notification feed, each matched to how that kind of update is acted on.

Reflection

The most important work happened before a single screen was drawn — deciding what mobile should and shouldn't do. Once that was set, the screen-level choices followed. The patterns here aren't isolated fixes; they're one principle applied consistently: mobile is for action, not administration. Every decision — the scoped navigation, the single-sheet actions, the role-based home screens — traces back to it.

Holding that line is what separates a useful mobile companion from a cluttered desktop squeezed into a smaller frame.

The designs weren't validated through formal usability testing — they were validated by shipping. IENT is live and in active use by procurement teams, and the decisions held up in production.
